new_statements.quote: Du point de vue phonologique, l'asama se distingue par un système tonal riche, ainsi que par la présence de voyelles longues qui ont une grande influence sur le schéma tonal des mots. [EN abstract, same record:] From the phonological point of view, Asama is characterized by a rich word-tone system, as well as long vowels that have a great influence on words' tone pattern. [...] It is based on first hand data collected by the author during fieldwork (for a total of more than 23 hours of fully transcribed and glossed natural texts and conversations, with tones explicitely marked).
new_statements.translation: From the phonological point of view, Asama stands out for a rich tone system, as well as for the presence of long vowels that have a great influence on the tonal pattern of words.

new_statements.quote: Asama is also characterized by a word-tone system where melodies are mapped onto whole word forms (Uwano 1977, Hayata 1995, Lawrence 2015, Uwano 2016), and there is a strong interdependence between tone pattern and syllable weight, as will be seen in the following sections. Inflected forms of verbs show four distinctive tone patterns: H, LH, HL and LHL. [...] (1) a. H: all syllables are high, except the last one if it is light; [p. 20–21:] First, in Asama, a word cannot begin with a high tone and end with a light syllable bearing a high tone, so that there is no *XCV H form with a high tone on every syllable, and *CV H forms are also banned due to a minimality constraint. If a word begins with a high tone, then a sequence of final light syllables is automatically low

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-tone system: a melody (H, LH, HL, LHL in inflected verbs) is assigned to the whole word form; realisation depends on syllable weight (heavy = CVV/CVC), e.g. a word-initial H forces final light syllables to be low, and *CV(H) is banned by a minimality constraint. No mention of stress anywhere in the article.
new_statements.exceptions: Neutralisation of H vs HL on forms beginning with H and ending in light syllables (§5.3.3); interdependence of vowel length and tone.

new_statements.quote: [p. 136–137, on Uwano 1977's analysis:] 氏のこの分析によれば、この方言は音節単位ではあるが、高く始る単語声調'a'（上野氏の高起「式」）と低く始る単語声調'b'（同じく低起式）およびピッチの変り目(高起式の場合は下がり目、低起式の場合は上がり目)の位置が問題になる狭義のアクセント方言で […] 筆者がかつてこれを見て多少分析を試みてみたところ、どう見ても名詞は２型単語声調としか思えない [p. 138:] 筆者としては、（４）の体系は、まず名詞に限れば（動詞については活用表が完備していないと何とも言えない)、（５）のように非常にあっさりした２型単語声調体系に過ぎないということである。 [p. 143:] それでも松原はもとより、浅間の名詞アクセントの体系も単語声調であると筆者は思っている。
new_statements.translation: [p. 136–137:] According to his [Uwano's] analysis, this dialect, though syllable-based, is an accent dialect in the narrow sense in which what matters is a high-beginning word tone 'a' (Uwano's high-register 'shiki') versus a low-beginning word tone 'b' (low register), plus the position of the pitch change (a fall in the high register, a rise in the low register) […] When I once tried analysing this myself, the nouns look to me like nothing other than a two-pattern word-tone system. [p. 138:] In my view the system in (4), at least if restricted to nouns (nothing can be said about verbs without complete paradigms), is no more than a very simple two-pattern word-tone system as in (5). [p. 143:] Even so, I believe that the noun accent system of Asama, like that of Matsubara, is word tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Asama nouns have two word tones (high-beginning vs low-beginning register); the pitch shape of a word is predicted from its word tone plus its syllable structure (every independent word contains at least one heavy syllable). Hayata re-analyses Uwano 1977's register + pitch-change-locus (accent-like) account as a two-pattern word-tone system. Stress is never mentioned; the whole discussion is about pitch (アクセント in the Japanese sense = pitch accent/tone).
new_statements.exceptions: Hayata notes forms in Uwano's table (4) marked * or × that do not occur among nouns; some pitch shapes are not predictable from word tone + syllable structure (marked * in his table (6)); verbs and adjectives left aside for lack of complete paradigms.

new_statements.quote: [p. 1:] ごく少数の単語を除き、浅間方言の各語形は少なくとも一つの重音節（長母音か二重母音を含むか、撥音か促音で終る音節）がなければならない。重音節の位置と音調型を基準にすると浅間方言の多くの単純名詞は共時的に次の三つの語類に分類できる｡ [p. 2:] 浅間方言のA語類の単語は語頭から高く、第二拍を含む音節は重音節である。B語類は語末音節が重音節で、四拍以下の単語の場合は語末拍が、五拍の単語の場合は語末音節が高い。C語類は前語末拍を含む音節が重音節で、四拍以下の単語の場合は語末拍が、五拍の単語の場合は語末音節が高い｡
new_statements.translation: [p. 1:] Apart from a very small number of words, every word form of the Asama dialect must contain at least one heavy syllable (a syllable containing a long vowel or diphthong, or ending in a moraic nasal or geminate). On the basis of the position of the heavy syllable and the tone pattern, most simple nouns of the Asama dialect can be classified synchronically into the following three word classes. [p. 2:] Words of class A in the Asama dialect are high from the beginning of the word, and the syllable containing the second mora is heavy. In class B the word-final syllable is heavy, and the final mora (for words of four or fewer moras) or the final syllable (for five-mora words) is high. In class C the syllable containing the penultimate mora is heavy, and the final mora (four or fewer moras) or the final syllable (five-mora words) is high.

new_statements.relation_note: Not in the 'works' list (held by the project from 2026-09-16). Same variety (浅間, Amagi town, Tokunoshima). Adds weight-conditioned three-class noun tone; compatible with Hayata's two-register analysis (Lawrence's A = high register; B and C = low register split by heavy-syllable position).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level tone: nouns fall into three classes defined jointly by where the obligatory heavy syllable sits and by the pitch pattern — A = high-register (high from the first syllable; Lawrence argues in §2 that whether it later falls is predictable, so high-register is a single pattern, 一型); B and C = low-register with the rise on the final mora (≤4 moras) or final syllable (5 moras). Foot structure (moraic trochee / iambic feet) is used to derive compound and diminutive tone. No mention of stress.
new_statements.exceptions: 'A very small number of words' lack a heavy syllable; minimal pairs like ha[n]dai 阪大 vs ha[n]dai 飯台 among high-register nouns, which Lawrence argues are predictable from structure; diminutives in -gama of class-A (C)Vi monosyllables and (C)VCV: disyllables become low-register.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Asama dialect (浅間, Amagi-chō 天城町, Tokunoshima). Hayata 1995 §1 (pp. 132–136) concerns the neighbouring Matsubara 松原 dialect, which he explicitly says is not the same system; only his §2 applies to toku1246. Lévêque & Pellard's data combine Okamura et al. 2009 / Uwano 2001 with Lévêque's own 2018–2019 fieldwork in Asama village.

readall_conflicts: No source mentions word stress, so there is no conflict about stress. The sources differ in how they analyse the pitch system: Uwano 1977 (as reported by Hayata 1995, pp. 136–137) treats Asama as an accent dialect in the narrow sense with two registers (high-beginning vs low-beginning) plus a distinctive locus of pitch change; Hayata 1995 (pp. 137–138, 143) rejects this and calls it a two-pattern word-tone system where the pitch shape follows from word tone plus syllable structure; Lawrence 2016 (pp. 1–2) sorts nouns into three classes A/B/C by heavy-syllable position and pitch, treating the high register as a single pattern; Lévêque & Pellard 2019/2023 and the Lévêque 2021 thesis abstract call it a word-tone system with four verbal melodies (H, LH, HL, LHL) conditioned by syllable weight. All agree it is a word-level pitch/tone system interacting with syllable weight, and none uses the category 'stress'.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both the deciding passage (Uwano 2015 sec. 3 p.179) and the supporting register-preservation passage (Uwano 2014 sec. 4 p.143; heavy-syllable definition p.142) are verbatim in the held NINJAL PDFs/text layers at the stated locators. (2) The classification 'tonal' (qv tonal-OR-pitch accent, no stress domain) rests on first-hand accent reports by Uwano, the primary fieldworker on this dialect since 1977; every other source opened — Hayata 1995 ('単語声調方言'), Lawrence 2016 (three lexical tone classes A/B/C, 高起/低起), Lévêque & Pellard 2023 ('word-tone system where melodies are mapped onto whole word forms.. strong interdependence between tone pattern and syllable weight'), and Kato 2022 for the neighbouring Isen dialect ('pitch accent language where H and L are distinguished') — confirms a lexical word-tone/pitch accent system with an obligatory heavy syllable and no stress. sources.quote: [2] Asama · endangered variety of Amami Ryukyuan · spoken in the Asama village of Tokunoshima Island, Japan · a few hundred of speakers, most > 70 years old · SOV, dependent-marking · word-tone, light vs. heavy syllables (CVV, CVC)
sources.note: Not in the 'works' list (held by the project from 2026-09-16). Same characterisation as Lévêque & Pellard 2023 and the thesis abstract: word-tone language, no stress statement.

sources.citation: Lawrence, Wayne (2016 [cited 2015]) 'Tokunoshima Asama hōgen no meishi onchō ni tsuite nidai: kōki onchō to shishō gokei no onchō' [Two topics on noun tone in the Asama dialect of Tokunoshima], Ryūkyū no Hōgen 40: 1-17, doi:10.15002/00013673
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Every Asama word form must contain at least one heavy syllable; simple nouns fall into three lexical tone classes A (high from word onset, 2nd-mora syllable heavy), B and C (low-beginning, final mora/syllable high, distinguished by position of the heavy syllable); discusses whether the high-register (高起) class has one or two contrastive patterns. Tone ('音調') throughout; no stress.
sources.locator: sec. 1.1 '単純名詞の音調と音節の軽重' p.1-2

sources.citation: Lawrence, Wayne ローレンス・ウエイン (2016 [cited as 2015]) 徳之島浅間方言の名詞音調について二題 — 高起音調と指小語形の音調 [Two topics on the noun tone of the Asama dialect of Tokunoshima: high-register tone and the tone of diminutive forms]. Ryūkyū no hōgen 琉球の方言 40: 1–17. doi:10.15002/00013673.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: [p. 1:] ごく少数の単語を除き、浅間方言の各語形は少なくとも一つの重音節（長母音か二重母音を含むか、撥音か促音で終る音節）がなければならない。重音節の位置と音調型を基準にすると浅間方言の多くの単純名詞は共時的に次の三つの語類に分類できる｡ [p. 2:] 浅間方言のA語類の単語は語頭から高く、第二拍を含む音節は重音節である。B語類は語末音節が重音節で、四拍以下の単語の場合は語末拍が、五拍の単語の場合は語末音節が高い。C語類は前語末拍を含む音節が重音節で、四拍以下の単語の場合は語末拍が、五拍の単語の場合は語末音節が高い｡
sources.locator: §1.1 単純名詞の音調と音節の軽重, pp. 1–2; §2 p. 6
sources.note: Not in the 'works' list (held by the project from 2026-09-16). Same variety (浅間, Amagi town, Tokunoshima). Adds weight-conditioned three-class noun tone; compatible with Hayata's two-register analysis (Lawrence's A = high register; B and C = low register split by heavy-syllable position).

sources.citation: Hayata Teruhiro 早田輝洋 (1995) 徳之島天城町松原と浅間の方言の名詞アクセント体系 — 単語声調方言の例として [The noun accent systems of the Matsubara and Asama dialects of Amagi, Tokunoshima: as examples of word-tone dialects]. Ryūkyū no hōgen 琉球の方言 18/19: 132–144. doi:10.15002/00012659.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: [p. 136–137, on Uwano 1977's analysis:] 氏のこの分析によれば、この方言は音節単位ではあるが、高く始る単語声調'a'（上野氏の高起「式」）と低く始る単語声調'b'（同じく低起式）およびピッチの変り目(高起式の場合は下がり目、低起式の場合は上がり目)の位置が問題になる狭義のアクセント方言で […] 筆者がかつてこれを見て多少分析を試みてみたところ、どう見ても名詞は２型単語声調としか思えない [p. 138:] 筆者としては、（４）の体系は、まず名詞に限れば（動詞については活用表が完備していないと何とも言えない)、（５）のように非常にあっさりした２型単語声調体系に過ぎないということである。 [p. 143:] それでも松原はもとより、浅間の名詞アクセントの体系も単語声調であると筆者は思っている。
sources.locator: §2 浅間方言 pp. 136–138 (quotes from p. 137 and p. 138); §3 おわりに p. 143
sources.note: Not in the 'works' list (held by the project from 2026-09-16). Section 1 (Matsubara dialect, pp. 132–136) describes a different Tokunoshima variety a few km away, which Hayata says is not the same system; only §2 is about Asama. Adds type (word tone, two noun classes) to an empty catalog rule; also records the Uwano 1977 alternative analysis (register + accent locus).

sources.citation: Hayata, Teruhiro (1995) 'Tokunoshima Amagi-chō Matsubara to Asama no hōgen no meishi akusento taikei: tango seichō hōgen no rei to shite' [The noun accent systems of the Matsubara and Asama dialects, Amagi, Tokunoshima: as examples of word-tone dialects], Ryūkyū no Hōgen 18/19: 132-144, doi:10.15002/00012659
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Reanalyses Uwano 1977's Asama data: Uwano treats it as high-beginning vs low-beginning word-tone (式) plus a pitch-turn locus; Hayata argues the nouns form 'a very simple two-pattern word-tone system' (非常にあっさりした２型単語声調体系). Either analysis is lexical tone/pitch-accent, not stress.
sources.locator: sec. 2 '浅間方言' pp.136-137 and (5) '浅間方言の名詞のアクセント体系'
